title: Component names a small team can say
excerpt: Name a component by the job it does: button, field, price row, dialog. Names based on color or size break the day the brand changes, which is when you need them most.
alt: A white modernist building with stacked cubic volumes and tall windows against a pale sky, parts a person can name by the job each volume does.
caption: Stacked volumes and tall windows. Name the part by its job. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How should a small team name interface components?
faqs.answer: Name the job, in words the team already says out loud. Button, field, and price row survive a new color. Blue card, big button, and header v2 do not. If the name needs a glossary, it is the wrong name.

faqs.question: Should every state be its own component?
faqs.answer: No. Error is a state of a field, not a separate species called error field. Promoting every state into the catalog makes a library nobody browses, and the styles drift. Write the states in the sentence that defines the component.

faqs.question: What if the design file and the code use different names?
faqs.answer: Pick one word and change both in the same week. A Figma component called price row and a code component called GreenCard is the old problem with better stationery. Tell the team in a sentence, and drop the alias once reviews use the new name.

markdown:
Name a component by the job it does. Button, field, price row, dialog, site header. Those names survive a new color, a new radius, and a new designer. Naming ui components by the look, "blue card" or "rounded banner," fails on the day the brand changes, which is the day you most need the name to keep working.

A small team has to say the name out loud in a review. If the name needs a glossary, it is the wrong name.

## The job, said in the customer's verb

Ask what the person is doing. Sending a form. Choosing a plan. Closing a layer. Scanning a price. The component name should be the thing they would recognize if they heard it across a table.

Button. Not "primary pill." The variants can be primary and quiet, if you truly need both. The object is still a button. Field. Not "underline input." The line is a style. The field is the job. Price row. Not "green savings strip." The green will change. The row that tells someone what they will pay will not.

Use words the team already says. If everyone says "the tray" for the panel that slides in from the edge, tray is a fine name, as long as you write one sentence defining it. If half the team says tray and half says drawer, pick one this week. Synonyms are how two components get built.

Avoid names that include the page. "Homepage hero" is a layout, and it tempts people to use it only there, or to duplicate it as "pricing hero" with the same structure. If it is a page intro with a heading, a sentence, and one action, call it a page intro. The homepage can use it. So can a feature page.

Hanabi keeps this list small on purpose. A marketing site and a light product surface can live on a short set: type styles, a button, a field, a link, a card only if the card is truly a repeated object, navigation, footer, and a dialog. More than that needs a reason. Got Next, Leadly, and Trade Moai are public product interfaces where the value is scanability. Extra component names work against that. Every new name is something the team has to remember while they are trying to ship.

## Names that break

Look breaks. "Blue card" dies when the card becomes cream. "Big button" dies when you change the scale. "Left nav" dies when it moves to the top on a marketing page. "Desktop table" dies on the phone, where you still need the same information.

Temporary breaks. "New header," "header v2," and "header final" will still be in the file next year, and nobody will know which one is real. Version numbers belong in the history of the file, not in the name. If you are replacing a header, replace it, and keep the name "header."

Personality breaks. "Magic banner," "delight toast," and "wow modal" feel friendly in a workshop and useless in a bug report. A bug report needs a noun. "The dialog does not return focus to the button that opened it" is a sentence a developer can fix. "The wow does not wow" is not.

Framework breaks, if you let them leak into the design language. A React name and a Figma name can match. They do not need to match a library's internal class. Tailwind utilities are an implementation. The team should say "price row," not a string of classes. Prisma models and PostgreSQL tables have their own names on the data side. Do not force the button to share a name with a database row. Different jobs.

Initials break. "CTA," used as a component, hides whether you mean a button, a band, or a whole section. Say the object. You can still talk about the action. The component has to be a thing you can point at.

## A small vocabulary, written down

Write the list on one page. Name. One sentence. The variants that exist. The variants that do not. "Dialog: a layer that interrupts, holds one task, and must be dismissible. We do not have a second size." That sentence prevents a "large dialog" from appearing because a stakeholder had a long form.

Put the list where the team will meet it. The front of the Figma file. A short page in the repo. On a Hanabi project, the client portal holds docs and brand files after delivery, which is a good home for the list so it does not live only in someone's head. The site itself, in Next.js and TypeScript, should use the same words in the code that the file uses in the layers. Renaming is cheap early and miserable after twenty pages.

Read the list aloud. If you stumble, the name is wrong. If two entries need a paragraph to explain the difference, you may have one component with a variant, or you may have a distinction that is not earning its keep. Merge them.

Include states in the sentence when the state is the point of confusion. "Field, with error" is a state of field, not a component called error field. Teams that promote every state to a component end up with a catalog nobody browses. They detach pieces and the error style drifts.

Agree on the verbs for actions inside the names you already have. "Save," "Continue," "Cancel" are labels, not components. Keep labels out of the component name. A button labeled Continue is still a button. This sounds obvious until a file fills up with ContinueButton, SaveButton, and CancelLink as if they were different species.

Say the name in design reviews before you say the hex value. "The field's error is too quiet" starts a useful conversation. "Make the red a bit redder" starts a paint conversation that leaves the component unnamed. On a small team the review is the documentation. If the name is not spoken, it will not be maintained, and the next page will invent a cousin. Pick names you are willing to say when a client is on the call, not only names that amuse the people who drew the file.

## How a name helps the build and the review

A shared name shortens the meeting. "The price row wraps on a phone" is a locate-and-fix. "The thing under the title, no, the other thing" is a twenty-minute tour of the file. Small teams do not have a design-systems department to absorb that tour. The name is the department.

A shared name makes scope visible. If a request introduces a new object, you can say so. "That is a new component. Swap or later phase." If it is a variant of a button, you can say that too, and resist a new species. The scope you agreed depends on this honesty. Vague names make every request sound small.

A shared name helps QA. The checklist can say "dialog, field, empty state" and mean the same thing to design and engineering. The WCAG principles, perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust, land on those objects. An understandable interface uses names, on screen and in code, that match the job. An operable one has a focus state on the thing you called a button. When the name is "blob," nobody writes the QA line, and the blob ships without a keyboard path.

It also helps the next person. Freelancers, a new founder, a new engineer, all inherit the vocabulary or invent a parallel one. Parallel vocabularies are how a second button style appears. Spend an hour on the list when you hire. It is cheaper than a visual audit in six months.

## When a new screen arrives

A new screen is a test of the vocabulary. Before anyone draws a new component, list the jobs on that screen in the names you already have. Page intro, field, button, price row, dialog. Most screens are a sentence made of old words. The newness is the content, not the species.

If a job is genuinely new, add one name and write the one-sentence definition the same day. "Tray: the panel that holds one task and can be closed without losing the page under it." Then stop. A screen that introduces four new names has not been reduced yet. Reduce it in Figma before it becomes four new React components. Renaming after the build is how "blue card" survives in the codebase under a nicer layer name.

Ask the engineer to read the list before they start. If they cannot point at each name in the file, the handoff is incomplete. If they want a different word, decide it now, in both places. A design name and a code name that diverge will be the thing the next review argues about, instead of the layout. Small teams do not have spare meetings for that argument.

Campaigns and one-off landing pages do not get to mint vocabulary either. They compose the page intro, the button, and a photograph. When the month ends, the composition goes away and the names remain. That is the point of naming the job. The look was always going to change.

## What to do with the names you already have

Export a list of components and layer names. Highlight every name that includes a color, a size adjective, a page, or a version. Those are the candidates. Do not rename the whole file in one heroic afternoon if the site is mid-build. Rename the ones you will touch this month, and stop creating new bad names today.

When you rename, update the code and the file together. A Figma component called "price row" and a React component called "GreenCard" is the old problem with better stationery. One pull request can rename the code. One page in the file can rename the source. Tell the team in a sentence, not in a manifesto.

Keep a one-line alias for a week if people will be lost. "Price row, formerly green card." Delete the alias once the reviews use the new name. Aliases that live forever become a second glossary.

Resist naming things after the client or the campaign. "Spring hero" is a campaign layout. If you need it, put it in a campaign page, built from the page intro and a photograph, and delete it when the campaign ends. The vocabulary of the product should still be intact in May.

If a landing page is starting to grow its own private language, ask whether it should have been a product screen. A page of benefits with names like "spark tile" is often a sign you were afraid to show the product. The piece on [when a landing page should be a product screen](/blog/when-a-landing-page-should-be-a-product-screen) is the next read if the vocabulary is getting cute because the real interface is missing.

You can see a short, job-based set of offers, which is a cousin of this discipline, in [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Each one is named for the work, not for a mood. Components deserve the same courtesy.
